screens.title: Connecting Frontend to the Blockchain
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting a web frontend to the blockchain is the essential bridge between your user interface and the user's wallet. In this lesson you will learn how a browser wallet like MetaMask exposes an injected object that your code can detect, how to initialize an Ethers. js Web3 provider using that injected object, and how to request the user’s account permission to perform signed transactions. You will also learn how to listen for the most important wallet events — account changes, network switches, and disconnects — and why handling those events keeps your dApp correct and secure. For example, when a user switches accounts, your UI must update the active address and signer; when the user switches networks, your contract addresses or network-dependent logic may no longer be valid. We will walk through concrete code patterns for detection, connect requests, provider and signer initialization, and robust error handling, and we’ll highlight common mistakes you should avoid, such as asking for private keys or failing to check chain IDs. By the end, you will be able to implement a connection flow that is safe, responsive, and predictable for users.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.3 › Skills and Safety
Skills and Safety Practices
Practical Safety Rules
  • Never request or transmit private keys; all signing must happen inside the wallet's secure signer.
  • Always check the connected chain's chainId or network name and inform the user when it differs from your contracts' network.
  • Handle user rejection (error code 4001) gracefully and do not retry without explicit consent.
  • Remove event listeners on unmount to avoid memory leaks or duplicate handlers.
Example
If a user switches MetaMask from Sepolia to Mainnet, the chainId will change. Your app should detect the change and either reload or re-initiate contract instances to avoid sending transactions to the wrong network.
Quick Checklist
window.ethereum present • Initialize BrowserProvider • Request eth_requestAccounts • getSigner after approval • Listen for accountsChanged/chainChanged • Clean up listeners on unmount

screens.title: Detecting a Wallet Provider (window.ethereum)
screens.narratorSegment: Detection is the first obvious but essential step for any dApp: you must know whether a wallet provider is present before attempting blockchain interaction. The standard convention is that an extension like MetaMask injects a global object, window. ethereum, into the browser. Practically this means your app checks if window. ethereum exists on component mount and uses that presence to decide whether to initialize a provider or present an install prompt. A simple check might set an error state and display a friendly message directing the user to install a wallet if none is found. A common misconception is assuming all browsers or environments include a provider; server-side rendering or private browsing sessions can be missing that object. As a concrete example, inside a React useEffect you check if (window. ethereum) then create an ethers. BrowserProvider; otherwise set an error string explaining the missing wallet and the recommended action. This prevents attempts to call provider methods that would throw and avoids confusing the user. Takeaway: always gate blockchain calls behind provider detection so your dApp degrades gracefully. Detecting a Wallet Provider (window.ethereum) means check window.ethereum on load; if absent, prompt installation and avoid calling provider apis.. In practical terms, how to confirm a browser wallet is available and guide the user when it is not. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
Detect window.ethereum
Confirm whether a browser wallet is injected so your app can safely initialize a provider or show guidance to install one.
Detection Snippet
useEffect(() => {
  if (window.ethereum) {
    // safe to initialize provider later
  } else {
    setError('MetaMask or other Web3 wallet not detected. Please install one.');
  }
}, []);
Concrete example: If window.ethereum is undefined in a user's browser, show a short help message and a link to wallet install instructions. Don't attempt provider calls or request accounts.
Key Takeaway

A detection check prevents runtime errors and gives users a clear next step when no wallet is installed.

Why it matters
Many errors arise from calling provider APIs when no wallet is present. Detecting the provider keeps your dApp robust and user friendly.
Common Mistake
Assuming window.ethereum is always present — this causes exceptions in environments without injected wallets or during server-side rendering.
Check Your Understanding
What should your UI show if window.ethereum is absent? A clear install guide and no wallet-specific controls until the user installs or connects a wallet.

screens.title: Create an Ethers.js BrowserProvider
screens.narratorSegment: After you detect an injected wallet object, the next step is to initialize a provider that your dApp will use to interact with the blockchain. In Ethers. js the recommended pattern for browser wallets is to create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum. This provider acts as an adapter: it forwards JSON-RPC requests to the wallet and returns results in a standard format. Importantly, the BrowserProvider itself does not sign transactions; after the user grants access you obtain a Signer from the provider that can sign. A concrete example: const ethProvider = new ethers. BrowserProvider(window. ethereum); setProvider(ethProvider); This lets you call provider. getNetwork() to detect which chain the wallet is connected to. A common misconception is to treat the provider as a signer; they are different roles. The provider handles read and some write requests routed through the wallet, while the signer performs actions that require the user's private key. Takeaway: initialize the BrowserProvider immediately after detection and use it to query network and create a signer only after permission is granted. Create an Ethers.js BrowserProvider means browserprovider forwards rpc through the wallet; getsigner() yields the account-capable signer after approval.. In practical terms, what the provider does and how it forwards requests through the wallet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Provider vs Signer
keyIdea.text: BrowserProvider forwards RPC through the wallet; getSigner() yields the account-capable signer after approval.

content.html:
Core Concept
Initialize an Ethers Provider
Create an adapter that routes your dApp's blockchain calls through the user's wallet provider.
Example Code
// Create a BrowserProvider from the injected object
const ethProvider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
setProvider(ethProvider);

// Later you can check the network
const currentNetwork = await ethProvider.getNetwork();
setNetwork(currentNetwork.name);
Use the provider for read-only calls and for acquiring signer after the user grants access. Do not assume the provider can sign transactions without a signer.
Key Takeaway

BrowserProvider standardizes RPC forwarding through the wallet; check network details via getNetwork() and use getSigner() only after account access.

Why this matters
Using BrowserProvider ensures your app uses the same transport and permission model as the user's wallet, avoiding low-level RPC differences between wallets and nodes.
Misconception
Treating the provider as the signer leads to attempts to sign without permission. Always request accounts and get a signer for signing operations.

screens.title: Requesting Account Access (eth_requestAccounts)
screens.narratorSegment: Requesting account access is the explicit consent step that allows your dApp to read accounts and obtain a signer for signing operations. The widely used method is to call window. ethereum. request with method eth_requestAccounts. In practice, implement a connectWallet function that first verifies a provider exists, then calls the request method and sets the returned account as the active account. You should wrap the call in try/catch to handle two important cases: user rejection and unexpected errors. When the user clicks 'Reject' in the wallet prompt, many wallets return an error object with code 4001. Handle this by showing a clear, friendly message and not proceeding to signing or further requests. For other errors, show a generic error message that includes the error message to aid troubleshooting. A concrete example from the chapter shows setting account, calling provider. getSigner to obtain a signer, and provider. getNetwork to store network info. Takeaway: requesting accounts must be explicit, handled asynchronously, and must gracefully respect a user's choice to deny access. Requesting Account Access (eth_requestAccounts) means use eth_requestaccounts, handle error code 4001 for rejection, and obtain a signer only after successful approval.. In practical terms, implementing connectwallet and handling user decision errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Explicit user consent
keyIdea.text: Use eth_requestAccounts, handle error code 4001 for rejection, and obtain a signer only after successful approval.

content.html:
Process
connectWallet
Request permission from the user and initialize signer and network state on success.
const connectWallet = async () => {
  if (!provider) { setError('No Ethereum provider found. Please install MetaMask.'); return; }
  try {
    const accounts = await window.ethereum.request({ method: 'eth_requestAccounts' });
    setAccount(accounts[0]);
    const currentSigner = await provider.getSigner();
    setSigner(currentSigner);
    const currentNetwork = await provider.getNetwork();
    setNetwork(currentNetwork.name);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.code === 4001) setError('Wallet connection rejected by user.');
    else setError('Error connecting to wallet: ' + err.message);
  }
};
Example & UX
If the user rejects, show a neutral message explaining the action is optional and provide a retry button in your UI. If connection succeeds, immediately show the connected address and network name so the user knows the app's context.
Common Mistake
Not handling the rejection error (4001) causes confusing states where the UI waits for an account that never arrives. Always set a clear error state in this case.
Pro Tip

After successful connect, immediately cache the network name and account in local state so renders remain stable while other initialization continues.

screens.title: Signer: What It Is and How to Use It
screens.narratorSegment: A Signer is the object representing an account capable of signing transactions and messages. In Ethers. js you obtain it from the provider after the user has granted account access. The provider alone is used for read operations and for forwarding signed requests, but signing requires the Signer because it has access to the user's account in the wallet. For example, after calling eth_requestAccounts and setting the account state, you typically call provider. getSigner() to retrieve the signer instance. That signer can then be passed to contract factories or used to sign transactions. A common misconception is that the Signer exposes private keys; it does not. The Signer operates through the wallet's secure UI. A concrete example: after user approval, getSigner will return an object whose sendTransaction call prompts the wallet UI for confirmation. The takeaway is simple: use the provider for queries, and use the signer for any action that requires user authorization and cryptographic signatures. Respect the wallet's prompts and never log or transmit signing payloads insecurely. Signer: What It Is and How to Use It means signer performs cryptographic operations on behalf of the account after user approval; it never exposes private keys to the frontend.. In practical terms, why the signer matters and how to obtain it from the provider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Signer performs cryptographic operations on behalf of the account after user approval; it never exposes private keys to the frontend.

content.html:
Definition
Signer
An account-capable object used to sign transactions and messages via the wallet.
How to obtain
// After connect and provider initialization
const currentSigner = await provider.getSigner();
setSigner(currentSigner);

// Use signer to send transactions; the wallet will prompt the user
await currentSigner.sendTransaction({ to: someAddress, value: someValue });
Practical Example
When a user clicks a UI action to mint a token, call a contract method using a signer so the wallet shows a confirmation and the user explicitly authorizes on-chain changes.
Misconception
The signer does not export the private key to your JS environment. It sends signing requests to the wallet which handles the private key securely.
Key Takeaway

Treat getSigner as the gateway to user-authorized state changes; always obtain it only after eth_requestAccounts succeeds.

screens.title: Handling accountsChanged Events
screens.narratorSegment: When a user switches accounts inside their wallet, the wallet emits an accountsChanged event that your dApp can listen for. Responding to this event keeps the UI accurate and prevents actions from being taken with a stale signer or account state. A typical handler receives an array of accounts; if accounts. length is zero, the user has locked or disconnected their wallet and you should clear account and signer state and prompt them to reconnect. If a new account appears, update the account state and reinitialize the signer from the existing provider. Example behavior includes setting account to accounts[0], calling provider. getSigner() again, and clearing error messages. A common mistake is to ignore accountsChanged, which leads to mismatches where the displayed address doesn't match the wallet's active account. For a concrete example, show the new address in the UI immediately after the event and re-query any user-specific contract data. Final takeaway: listening for accountsChanged is inexpensive and dramatically improves correctness and user trust. Handling accountsChanged Events means update account and signer when accountschanged fires; clear state if no accounts are present.. In practical terms, keep your ui and signer in sync when the user switches accounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Update account and signer when accountsChanged fires; clear state if no accounts are present.

content.html:
Event
accountsChanged
React to account switches to preserve correctness of displayed address, signer, and user data.
const handleAccountsChanged = (accounts) => {
  if (accounts.length === 0) {
    setAccount(null);
    setSigner(null);
    setError('Please connect to MetaMask.');
  } else if (accounts[0] !== account) {
    setAccount(accounts[0]);
    if (provider) setSigner(provider.getSigner());
    setError('');
  }
};

window.ethereum.on('accountsChanged', handleAccountsChanged);
Concrete Example
A user switches from one address to another. Immediately re-query any balances or permissions tied to the previous address to ensure the UI reflects the new account.
Mistake to Avoid
Failing to update signer after accountsChanged leaves your app using the old signer, causing signing prompts to reference the incorrect account and confusing users.
Check Yourself

After handling accountsChanged, does your UI show the new address and recent account-specific data like token balances?

screens.title: Handling chainChanged and Network Validation
screens.narratorSegment: The chainChanged event indicates the wallet switched networks. Because smart contracts are deployed to specific networks, a network switch can render your contract instances invalid. Common practice is to respond to the event by reloading the page or by programmatically reinitializing provider, signer, and contract objects. The simplest robust response is to reload; many dApps do this because a code path expects a specific network. Alternatively, you can detect the new chainId and inform the user if your dApp does not support it, prompting them to switch back. For example, handleChainChanged might log the new chainId and call window. location. reload() to reset state. A misconception is to assume the same contract addresses apply on every network; they do not. As a concrete example, if a user switches from Sepolia to Mainnet, the web app must avoid submitting transactions intended for Sepolia addresses on Mainnet. Takeaway: always check chainId against your supported network and react to chainChanged to keep contract calls correct and safe. Event
disconnect
When the wallet disconnects, clear account-specific state and show a reconnect path.

  setSigner(null);

Not removing listeners on unmount can cause multiple invocations of handlers if the component mounts again, leading to duplicated state updates.

Remove listeners and reset state on disconnect so your app remains predictable and secure.

Implement Wallet Connection in App.jsx

Step-by-step

On connect: UI shows connected account and network name. On reject: friendly error appears. On account switch: account updates. On network change: app reloads or shows unsupported network message.

Test interactions in a live browser with MetaMask installed; follow the lifecycle and verify each event handler behaves as expected.

fullNarratorScript:
Connecting a web frontend to the blockchain is the essential bridge between your user interface and the user's wallet. In this lesson you will learn how a browser wallet like MetaMask exposes an injected object that your code can detect, how to initialize an Ethers. js Web3 provider using that injected object, and how to request the user’s account permission to perform signed transactions. You will also learn how to listen for the most important wallet events — account changes, network switches, and disconnects — and why handling those events keeps your dApp correct and secure. For example, when a user switches accounts, your UI must update the active address and signer; when the user switches networks, your contract addresses or network-dependent logic may no longer be valid. We will walk through concrete code patterns for detection, connect requests, provider and signer initialization, and robust error handling, and we’ll highlight common mistakes you should avoid, such as asking for private keys or failing to check chain IDs. By the end, you will be able to implement a connection flow that is safe, responsive, and predictable for users.

These objectives focus your work: first, you'll detect whether a user has a compatible wallet installed and guide them if not; second, you'll initialize an Ethers. js provider that forwards requests through the injected wallet; third, you'll implement a safe connect flow that requests account permissions and obtains a signer for signing; and fourth, you'll add robust listeners and error handling for account and network changes. Each objective pairs a concrete skill with why it matters. For example, detecting window. ethereum ensures your dApp doesn't attempt operations when no wallet is present and can provide clear guidance. Initializing a Web3 provider through Ethers. js standardizes how you call the blockchain and isolates wallet-specific details. Requesting accounts with eth_requestAccounts is the user consent step — a legal and security checkpoint — and handling accountsChanged and chainChanged keeps your UI in sync with the wallet's real state. Together they form a safe, user-focused connection layer for any dApp.

Beyond code, connecting a frontend to a wallet demands safety standards. You will learn to never ask for private keys and to rely on the wallet's signer for cryptographic operations. You will also practice validating the connected chain by checking chainId or the network name so your dApp doesn't attempt contract calls on the wrong chain. We will cover error codes you are likely to see, including the user-rejection error code, and how to surface friendly messages so users understand what happened and what to do next. Practicing these skills reduces support issues and prevents accidental or unsafe operations. Throughout the hands-on activity, we’ll reinforce the habit of graceful degradation: if a wallet isn't present, provide clear instructions rather than failing silently. These safety practices and UX conventions are as important as the code itself for successful dApps.

Detection is the first obvious but essential step for any dApp: you must know whether a wallet provider is present before attempting blockchain interaction. The standard convention is that an extension like MetaMask injects a global object, window. ethereum, into the browser. Practically this means your app checks if window. ethereum exists on component mount and uses that presence to decide whether to initialize a provider or present an install prompt. A simple check might set an error state and display a friendly message directing the user to install a wallet if none is found. A common misconception is assuming all browsers or environments include a provider; server-side rendering or private browsing sessions can be missing that object. As a concrete example, inside a React useEffect you check if (window. ethereum) then create an ethers. BrowserProvider; otherwise set an error string explaining the missing wallet and the recommended action. This prevents attempts to call provider methods that would throw and avoids confusing the user. Takeaway: always gate blockchain calls behind provider detection so your dApp degrades gracefully. Detecting a Wallet Provider (window.ethereum) means check window.ethereum on load; if absent, prompt installation and avoid calling provider apis.. In practical terms, how to confirm a browser wallet is available and guide the user when it is not. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After you detect an injected wallet object, the next step is to initialize a provider that your dApp will use to interact with the blockchain. In Ethers. js the recommended pattern for browser wallets is to create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum. This provider acts as an adapter: it forwards JSON-RPC requests to the wallet and returns results in a standard format. Importantly, the BrowserProvider itself does not sign transactions; after the user grants access you obtain a Signer from the provider that can sign. A concrete example: const ethProvider = new ethers. BrowserProvider(window. ethereum); setProvider(ethProvider); This lets you call provider. getNetwork() to detect which chain the wallet is connected to. A common misconception is to treat the provider as a signer; they are different roles. The provider handles read and some write requests routed through the wallet, while the signer performs actions that require the user's private key. Takeaway: initialize the BrowserProvider immediately after detection and use it to query network and create a signer only after permission is granted. Create an Ethers.js BrowserProvider means browserprovider forwards rpc through the wallet; getsigner() yields the account-capable signer after approval.. In practical terms, what the provider does and how it forwards requests through the wallet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Requesting account access is the explicit consent step that allows your dApp to read accounts and obtain a signer for signing operations. The widely used method is to call window. ethereum. request with method eth_requestAccounts. In practice, implement a connectWallet function that first verifies a provider exists, then calls the request method and sets the returned account as the active account. You should wrap the call in try/catch to handle two important cases: user rejection and unexpected errors. When the user clicks 'Reject' in the wallet prompt, many wallets return an error object with code 4001. Handle this by showing a clear, friendly message and not proceeding to signing or further requests. For other errors, show a generic error message that includes the error message to aid troubleshooting. A concrete example from the chapter shows setting account, calling provider. getSigner to obtain a signer, and provider. getNetwork to store network info. Takeaway: requesting accounts must be explicit, handled asynchronously, and must gracefully respect a user's choice to deny access. Requesting Account Access (eth_requestAccounts) means use eth_requestaccounts, handle error code 4001 for rejection, and obtain a signer only after successful approval.. In practical terms, implementing connectwallet and handling user decision errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Signer is the object representing an account capable of signing transactions and messages. In Ethers. js you obtain it from the provider after the user has granted account access. The provider alone is used for read operations and for forwarding signed requests, but signing requires the Signer because it has access to the user's account in the wallet. For example, after calling eth_requestAccounts and setting the account state, you typically call provider. getSigner() to retrieve the signer instance. That signer can then be passed to contract factories or used to sign transactions. A common misconception is that the Signer exposes private keys; it does not. The Signer operates through the wallet's secure UI. A concrete example: after user approval, getSigner will return an object whose sendTransaction call prompts the wallet UI for confirmation. The takeaway is simple: use the provider for queries, and use the signer for any action that requires user authorization and cryptographic signatures. Respect the wallet's prompts and never log or transmit signing payloads insecurely. When a user switches accounts inside their wallet, the wallet emits an accountsChanged event that your dApp can listen for. Responding to this event keeps the UI accurate and prevents actions from being taken with a stale signer or account state. A typical handler receives an array of accounts; if accounts. length is zero, the user has locked or disconnected their wallet and you should clear account and signer state and prompt them to reconnect. If a new account appears, update the account state and reinitialize the signer from the existing provider. Example behavior includes setting account to accounts[0], calling provider. getSigner() again, and clearing error messages. A common mistake is to ignore accountsChanged, which leads to mismatches where the displayed address doesn't match the wallet's active account. For a concrete example, show the new address in the UI immediately after the event and re-query any user-specific contract data. Final takeaway: listening for accountsChanged is inexpensive and dramatically improves correctness and user trust. The chainChanged event indicates the wallet switched networks. Because smart contracts are deployed to specific networks, a network switch can render your contract instances invalid. Common practice is to respond to the event by reloading the page or by programmatically reinitializing provider, signer, and contract objects. The simplest robust response is to reload; many dApps do this because a code path expects a specific network. Alternatively, you can detect the new chainId and inform the user if your dApp does not support it, prompting them to switch back. For example, handleChainChanged might log the new chainId and call window. location. reload() to reset state. A misconception is to assume the same contract addresses apply on every network; they do not. As a concrete example, if a user switches from Sepolia to Mainnet, the web app must avoid submitting transactions intended for Sepolia addresses on Mainnet. Takeaway: always check chainId against your supported network and react to chainChanged to keep contract calls correct and safe. This lesson highlights common pitfalls when connecting to wallets and shows practical fixes. First, not checking for window. ethereum will cause your app to throw when calling provider methods. The fix is to gate initialization behind a detection check. Second, failing to handle error code 4001 leaves users confused; handle it by showing a clear message and allowing retry rather than retrying automatically. Third, ignoring accountsChanged and chainChanged leads to stale UI and mismatched contract interactions; listen for these events and update account, signer, and network state appropriately. Fourth, mixing provider and signer responsibilities confuses your code; use provider for network queries and getSigner for signing actions.
